items.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Neon for fast coding and agent work
items.summary: Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 Neon scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (#3 overall), ranks #1 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), and scores 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1. It costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens with a 1 million-token context window, and is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and in the Gemini app. For developers it is another frontier option, available via API, built for long-running agent workflows and coding.

evidence.quote: Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level
The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.

items.title: OpenAI models improve chip designs, and AMD adopts some changes
items.summary: OpenAI says changes proposed by its models cut standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit of Jalapeño, its first custom inference chip, and were silicon proven. Working with AMD, it saw up to 14% improvement over heavily optimized baselines on flagship GPU IP, and AMD has put some changes into a design sent for manufacturing; on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score. Frontier models are now doing expert-level RTL work, verified with EDA tools such as Synopsys.

items.title: OpenAI: coding agents now finish nearly half of two-to-four-hour research tasks
items.summary: OpenAI's update on internal research acceleration finds that from March to October, estimated agent success rose from 23% to 46% on tasks needing two to four hours of human work, and from 13% to 35% on four-to-eight-hour tasks. The gains are uneven: autonomous success was 79% for monitoring training runs but 25% for writing inference and serving code, and OpenAI says humans remain a core part of the research loop. It is a first-hand read on what coding agents can and cannot yet do in real R&D.

evidence.quote: From March to October, estimated success rose from 23% to 46% for tasks estimated to require two to four hours of human work, and rose from 13% to 35% for tasks estimated to require four to eight hours.
the autonomous agent success rate was 79% for monitoring training runs, 35% for launching training runs, and 25% for writing code for inference and serving stacks.
Overall, uplift is jagged, and humans remain a core part of the AI research loop.

items.title: Anthropic: Claude Fable 5.2 solves two open problems in black hole physics
items.summary: Anthropic reports that Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems tied to black holes and quantum gravity: it completed a calculation physicists set up more than 20 years ago but never solved, showing a phase transition is abrupt, and it found and proved the precise ceiling for the simplest version of a technique used to rule out candidate theories. For the first problem, Claude ran a small research group of copies of itself and checked its math against known results. It is a concrete case of a model pushing long chains of scientific calculation forward.

evidence.quote: Claude Fable 5.2 solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved.

Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt.

Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered.

items.title: RadixArk releases DaisyRose-27B, an RL-tuned Qwen3.8-27B for agents
items.summary: RadixArk's first model, DaisyRose-27B, is built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using its open-source Miles framework on 1,200 curated long-horizon tasks, taking 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. It raises Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%, ships under Apache 2.0, and keeps the base model's architecture, tokenizer, chat template and 256K-token context window. It is an open-weights recipe for agent post-training with a small, high-quality task set.

evidence.quote: built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0

items.title: Reson8 open-sources Rumble-2-Flash, a 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages
items.summary: Rumble-2-Flash is a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages released under Apache 2.0; it averages a 6.96% error rate on the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track and reaches 7.86% WER on a 302-hour call-centre benchmark, versus 7.78% for NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B). It uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture, so it runs in Transformers or vLLM with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code, a good fit for cost- and speed-sensitive multilingual transcription.

items.title: Xing 4 report: training TeleChat's agentic models on Ascend 910C
items.summary: The Xing 4 report describes how this TeleChat-lineage model series co-designs architecture and training infrastructure for Ascend: a MindSpore HyperParallel stack supports pretraining a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, and post-training uses TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform with asynchronous execution and partial rollout. It is a rare end-to-end engineering reference for teams training large models on domestic chips.

items.title: FastFrames brings autoregressive video generation to interactive latency
items.summary: The paper finds that VAE decoding and KV cache updates account for over half of end-to-end latency and replaces them with lightweight alternatives: the 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame (28 RPS) on a single B200 while matching a state-of-the-art model nearly 8x slower, and the 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame on an 8x B200 node. That makes camera- and physics-conditioned video generation usable in real time.

items.title: Multi-Branch Transformer scales by branching and cuts KV cache up to 34%
items.summary: The Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT) runs independently parameterized branches of Transformer blocks in parallel between shared layers, and Joint-KV builds one shared KV cache per depth. At MoE scales from 0.8B to 2.1B, fitted scaling curves show standard Transformers need up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match its loss, while KV-cache storage drops by up to 34% and decoding throughput rises up to 51.4% on a single H200 GPU. Branching offers a third scaling axis besides width and depth.

evidence.quote: These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU.

items.title: Energy-Based Reasoners hit 99.9% on Sudoku-Extreme with 1.8M parameters
items.summary: Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs) learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and treat looped updates as gradient descent on it: the energy scores candidates without an external verifier, and the gradient guides refinement and signals when to stop. With only 1.8M parameters, EBRs reach 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model, pointing to recurrent reasoners that stop adaptively.

evidence.quote: With only 1.8M parameters, EBRs achieve 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model.
Its value scores candidate predictions without requiring an external verifier, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a natural signal for stopping.

items.title: OpenAI explains how the Codex sandbox constrains local commands
items.summary: Rather than VMs or containers, Codex uses each platform's own sandboxing facilities, such as Seatbelt on macOS, to limit filesystem and network access for commands in the user's existing environment; the default :workspace profile allows writes within the workspace, keeps .git and .codex read-only, and disables network access. The post also shows the codex sandbox command for testing permission profiles and an example of sandboxing an MCP server, useful for anyone building their own agent harness.

evidence.quote: Instead of moving computation to a separate environment to provide isolation, Codex uses each platform’s sandboxing facilities to constrain commands running in the user’s existing environment.
On macOS, Codex uses Seatbelt
Allows writes within the workspace, while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only.
Disables network access.
The Codex CLI provides a sandbox command to facilitate running an arbitrary command under a permission profile defined in the Codex config.
Example: sandboxing an MCP server

items.title: Running a 180B MoE model on a 32 GB Mac with Transformers
items.summary: On the Hugging Face blog, Tarek Ziadé shows MoE expert streaming in Transformers: only the experts the router picks are read from SSD into a bounded cache, which runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB MacBook M5 at ~14 tok/s, within 6% of the dedicated engine Strata. The generic implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, giving developers a way to run MoE models larger than memory without leaving Transformers.

evidence.quote: Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

items.title: Dharma-AI predicts fine-tuning time far better than FLOP math
items.summary: Across 272 production SFT jobs on NVIDIA H200 GPUs (about 7,382 GPU-hours), the usual FLOP-based estimate reached only R² = 0.31 with MAE 12.41 h, while a CatBoost regressor using only pre-dispatch information reached R² = 0.98, MAE 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h. The gap comes from signals such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy and per-GPU load, which teams running shared GPU clusters can use to schedule better.

evidence.quote: So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total

the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h
such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime
